results.title: Selecting Samples, Radiocarbon Dating Understood
results.content:
Title: Selecting Samples, Radiocarbon Dating Understood
University of Texas at AustinCollege of Liberal Arts. ## Texas Beyond History. Planning ahead, the archeologist can articulate questions to address, identify datable material types recovered from excavation (or pulled from curation), and select the most appropriate samples for dating. With the high-resolution measurement capabilities of AMS, context and sample identification became critical. Even better candidates for dating are annual seeds, nut shells, fruits, or leaves. Archeobotanists can also often identify tree species by looking at wood charcoal under magnification and consider the lifespan of those species. By dating short-lived “economic” species such as food remains, instead of the wood used to fuel the cooking fire, the archeologist can address questions about the use of specific food plants such as agave or corn. By sampling and dating fuelwood and economic species from a cooking feature context, for example, the archeologists can check for consistency between the dates. ### Sample Challenges. Problematic materials include aquatic organisms or animals that derived a large part of their diet from aquatic environments and therefore likely suffer from marine or freshwater reservoir effects (see In the Environment). Another common problem is the old wood effect, discussed above. While bone can be an excellent material to date, problems with poor collagen preservation in old or degraded bone can make obtaining dates difficult or impossible (see In the Lab). ### Replicating Assays. Replication can help identify mixed deposits, reservoir offsets, effects of different pretreatment methods, interlaboratory error, and the reuse of older materials. Such features may also contain items that date long after or before the cooking event(s), such as trash items discarded decades or centuries later. In fact, involving a radiocarbon scientist on the project team from the outset can greatly improve dating results. A fundamental step is to consider how the sample material relates to a targeted event or behavioral pattern of interest. Whether an archeologist has an ideal selection of samples to choose from or must do the best they can with problematic sample materials, the reasons for submitting a sample should be made explicit during reporting, along with discussion of any potential problems with it and any attempts to mitigate those problems.

results.title: Dealing with Outliers and Offsets in Radiocarbon Dating | Radiocarbon | Cambridge Core
results.content: The use of Bayesian statistics for the analysis of groups of dates is becoming a common way to integrate all of the 14C evidence together. In particular, there is an assumption that all of the 14C measurements are correct in their context and that the original 14C concentration of the sample is properly represented by the calibration curve. There is also a full treatment of outlier analysis for samples that are all of the same age, which takes account of the uncertainty in the calibration curve. In this paper, the use of a similar approach for other kinds of correlated offset (such as overall measurement bias or regional offsets in the calibration curve) is discussed and the implementation of these methods in OxCal v 4.0 is presented. results.title: (PDF) Marine reservoir effect on the Southeastern coast of Brazil: results from the Tarioba shellmound paired samples
results.content: # Marine reservoir effect on the Southeastern coast of Brazil: results from the Tarioba shellmound paired samples. On the Southeastern coast of Brazil the presence of many archaeological shellmounds offers a great potential for studying the radiocarbon marine reservoir effect (MRE). Radiocarbon dating of closely associated marine mollusk shells and terrestrial material (mammal bones or charred wood) collected from archaeological contexts in northern Atlantic Iberian coastal areas is used to quantify the marine14C reservoir effect (ΔR) for the coastal waters off the Cantabrian coast of northern Iberia. A regional marine reservoir correction (ΔR) of 33±24 14C yr for southern Brazil was obtained from 6 marine shell samples collected in the states of Santa Catarina and Paraná. The Usiminas shellmound on the Cabo Frio Island: Marine reservoir effect in an upwelling region on the coast of Brazil. In this kind of archaeological settlement, common on the southern and southeastern Brazilian coasts, marine mollusk shells are frequently used for radiocarbon dating and can represent a valuable tool in the study of MRE. This work aims to examine the possible upwelling influence on the paleoreservoir age of Brazilian surficial coastal waters based on paired terrestrial/marine samples obtained from archaeological remains. There are also significant age differences between carbonized seed samples (977 14 C yr) and marine samples (200 and 228 14 C yr) from the same archaeological layer that cannot be explained by a reservoir effect or an old-wood effect for charcoal. Marine Reservoir Corrections on the Southeastern Coast of Brazil: Paired Samples from the Saquarema Shellmound. Radiocarbon Reservoir corrections on the Brazilian coast from pre-bomb marine shells. Despite the great extent of the Brazilian coast, there are very few studies on the marine radiocarbon reservoir correction local offset (DR) for this region. Coeval shell and charcoal from Santa Catarina State, Brazil, differ systematically in (super 14) C content, indicating a reservoir effect in marine samples. This article assesses the potential use of terrestrial shells as representative of atmospheric carbon reservoir in the calculation of the marine reservoir effect (MRE) of the southeastern Brazilian coast.

results.title: A Pre-treatment Routine for Correcting Age-Offsets on AMS Radiocarbon Dated Ceramic Residue - ADS
results.content: ## A Pre-treatment Routine for Correcting Age-Offsets on AMS Radiocarbon Dated Ceramic Residue. Roper, from Kansas State University, and Dr. Linda Scott Cummings, from PaleoResearch Institute, will collaborate on a study designed to develop a pre-treatment protocol for correcting age-offsets on AMS radiocarbon dated ceramic residue. Charred food burned onto ceramic vessels during cooking, often termed ceramic residue, is one of the materials now commonly selected for dating and increasingly used in North America, Europe, and Asia. As its use increases, ceramic residue ages are often noted to be older than dates on other short-lived material from the same context, and thus are not accurate. AMS dates on residue and on context materials known to produce accurate ages will be paired to test the efficacy of the developing method. Project Outcomes: AMS radiocarbon dating annual plant remains and charred food residues on single-use pottery are the best methods to accurately date an archaeological site's occupation; however, there are some assumptions that need to be addressed. Were annual plant remains always available, "old wood" errors wouldn't occur; however, because annual plant fossils are rare, archaeologists use charred food crusts to date their "single-year-of-use." Pottery is abundant compared to annual macrofossils and contains charred food crust residues (CFC's), different from soluble food residues soaked into vessels, yielding "single-year-dates". Archaeologists assume food crust 14C dates are the pottery's exact year of use ¾ the archaeological occupation date. Our project goals were: 1) Determine causes for age offsets between CFCs and associated annual plants, 2) Test if older carbon contaminated charred food crust, 3) Identify chemical signatures indicating whether or not ancient carbon could be removed, and 4) test sherds from different regions and test multiple treatments on CFC from single sherds. Dating this charred food crust is different than dating dairy fatty acids that soak into ceramics and are recovered and separated for 14C dating (Casanova et al 2020). Dates on charred food crusts from different locations on a single cooking vessel vary by 100-500 years. Because food crust dates were usually older than dates on associated annual plants, we concluded that charred food crusts contain ancient carbon.
